text: Good afternoon. My name is Lauren Chernoff, and I am calling this Thursday, October 1st, 2026, Specialized Programs and Centers Committee meeting to order. We have no public comment today, so we will jump right into item 3.01, approval of the draft minutes for the September 15th, 2026, meeting. Mr. Pepper, are there any additions or changes to the minutes? There are not, Madam Chair. All right. With that, I will move to approve the draft minutes for the September

15th, 2026, meeting. Do I have a second? Second. All those in favor? Aye. Aye. And that passes with two zero, with one not here, Ms. Donahue, absent for the vote. So that passes. We will move on. All right. Next up, we have our first information item 4.01, review of Policy 5120, Alternative Education Programs. And joining us today is our Chief of Schools, Ms. Raye Mitchell. The floor is yours. Thank you. Good afternoon, committee members.

This afternoon, I am bringing forward Policy 5120, Alternative Education Programs, for its five-year review. Currently, we have expanded options to include settings designated as a program or a school, and therefore, in collaboration with the Department of Student Services, we changed the title from Alternative Education Programs to Alternative Education Settings.

Additionally, because these settings are no longer specific to only high school students, we revised the policy under the sections for credit and student eligibility to be changed accordingly. And enrollment, whether by self-referral or reassignment, is intended to provide continuous instruction from the student's home school to the alternative setting to include any accommodations for our EL students and/or our students with disabilities.

Are there any questions regarding the red line version? Mr. Pepper, any questions? Thank you, Madam Chair. So in the section, I believe it's 3D, on student eligibility, there's a whole lot of reasons that were taken out and a generalized clause of each alternative education setting has specific eligibility criteria put in as a replacement. Are we going to have an associated regulation that has a lot

of these listed in there? Or where can somebody find the reasoning that a student might need or benefit from a specific alternative setting? Thank you. So that section was removed because originally, or the policy as it currently is, and these reasons were for our high school students, which when we now have middle school students and even virtually we have elementary, this information was no longer applicable.

So while we do not currently have one that sets that aside because each setting has its own criteria that is listed for that information. So for example, if a student is self-referring to the North Star School, that has a set of criteria versus the RISE program, and so information for each alternative setting that is set forth for that particular program, which can be found at the home school through the counseling office and/or on the webpage.

Okay. Would it be something we'd want to mention where they could find the eligibility for a specific program in the policy? Just thinking ahead for as this goes probably next week or next month to action, that it just might be helpful if there's-- It could even be a regulation, just something to redirect people to the right spot so they know that, "Yes, the North Star School is a good fit for me," or, "Virtual Loudoun is a good fit for me."

So just a clarifying question. So are you asking to have a regulation that describes all of those different program settings or just a mention in this policy? I would actually perhaps neither. Perhaps it's a regulation that states specific criteria for- Okay ... each individual program can be found on their website or something that could be-- The reason I want a regulation is it's so much more fluid than a policy, right? We can update and change regulations as needed.

But something to knowing the purpose of these programs really help the public find the program that best fits the needs of their student. Understood. Thank you for that. And just to clarify, there is not a current regulation. Not for each individual program that encompasses that. So they- Okay. And I don't need an individual program, but I- Yeah. I understand exactly what you're saying. Yes. Thank you. Got you. I had a similar question along the same lines of just making sure that either we

cross-reference where that can be found or that we create a regulation. So appreciate that comment. And then did you have any other questions? Yeah. Okay. I had a question in the opening paragraph. You added the section that says students may be reassigned to alternative educational settings through the student discipline process, and then you go on to say a few other things. I'm totally fine with that because then in the bottom of the policy, it outlines that again.

But also in the policy that it's outlined about self-referral in terms of RISE. Would it be helpful to also put or self-referral in that opening paragraph so that both of them are mentioned? Because right now it just seems like that's the only reason you could be. That's the way it reads to me in the opening. Thank you for that comment. Yes, I can add some language to clarify that as the intention was to

address the fact that the only time students cannot self-refer, for example, is when it's discipline. They can self-refer through other things, but when it's discipline related, it is a reassignment. Okay. So for example, our TAPE program is through discipline. That's not a self-referral. Okay. I guess just because it's mentioned again in Section G about the discipline, but for some reason that got pulled into the intro paragraph, but the elective

enrollment didn't. So if we could just sort of like an intro paragraph would outline what those different options are. Yes. English teacher in me is- Got you. And then there is one other thing that I was wondering, and it's really nitpicky, so I apologize, but- It's okay ... in the section where under Goal, Section A, number one, it struck out in a suitable environment to best meet the unique needs of the student because

I believe that's what you're trying to achieve with the new sentence that's put there. Yes. But I don't see anywhere in the new sentence where it really addresses a suitable environment. I see that resources are addressed and personalized needs are addressed. Both are great, but I think the suitable environment piece is really key. So I would like to have that not removed. I can do an amendment and rewrite it for you, or we could just agree that that could be something that could be added.

What I can do is rewrite that, and I can send it to you, and if that agrees with the two of you, then we can do it that way and I'll add it in. Perfect. The only other thing, and this may be piggybacking, Madam Chair, off of what you said in the first paragraph. I don't actually even know because the opening paragraph really is two sentences. I don't even know if the second sentence is necessary about student reassignment at all because we talk about later on in the policy as we get down to Section F about

the method through which a student is in the program. I think really the opening paragraph is fine just as a sentence as to what alternative education settings are. Just ending it- Ending it at educational goals ... goals and take out the "students may be reassigned." Yeah, because you do outline it in the next section. I'd be fine with that. Makes it a little cleaner. Cleans it up. Mm-hmm. Okay, that works. Other than that, I think the substance of the policy is great, and it's great that we're updating it, and it's wonderful that we offer all these alternative settings.

So I don't have anything further if you don't. All right. Thank you. So we will move this to action next time. So we're going to send it out for feedback- Oh, yes, of course ... and bring it back fresh. And action. Yes. Thank you, Mr. Slevin. All right. Thank you so much, Ms. Mitchell. We appreciate you being here. And now we will move on to Item 4.02, Future Ready Lesson, the RISIG and Special Programs. And to present is Ms. Katie Clark, our Director of Academic Programs, and

Dr. Grubbs, Director of Career, Technical, and Adult Education. The floor is yours. Thank you so much. Good afternoon. We really appreciate the opportunity to share an update on our middle school Future Ready Lesson, which will take place on Thursday, November 12th. Dr. Grubbs and I are excited to provide an overview this afternoon about this district-wide experience

We will share reminders today about the new ACL testing process, provide an overview of the middle school future ready lesson, and allow time for questions, feedback, and considerations as we prepare for implementation. So as discussed during the June SBC meeting, we shared several updates on the ACL admissions process for this year. These changes are part of our ongoing efforts to strengthen access, consistency,

and overall student experience. First, students applying to the Academy of Science and Academy of Engineering and Technology will continue to participate in that STEM thinking assessment. We did work with our partner, Insight Assessment, to develop that custom ACL admissions assessment designed specifically for our programs. This assessment will continue to measure critical thinking, problem-solving, and STEM-related reasoning skills that align with the expectations and learning experience within these programs.

Additionally, we are also moving to that single testing day, November 12th, for all middle school applicants. This change is intended to create a more equitable and efficient process for students and families while reducing barriers to participation. So students enrolled in LCPS middle schools will test in their home school environment while home school and private school students will test at the Academies of Loudoun on that same day. So while that is happening,

while our eighth grade ACL applicants are testing on that day, the rest of the students, sixth, seventh, and non-testing eighth-grade students will participate in our first ever middle school future ready exploration lesson. This lesson is being developed through a collaborative effort between academic programs, career and technical education, school counseling, and additional partners across LCPS. Using the Riasec framework, students will participate in

guided reflection to explore LCPS programs and make connections between their strengths, interests, and future goals. So some logistics. For this day, the lesson is going to allow us to expand access to information about LCPS programs and ensure every middle school student, sixth, seventh, and eighth, have the opportunity to explore the pathways available to them. Using the Riasec framework and SchooLinks, students will engage in guided

reflection that helps them connect their strengths, interests, and aspirations to future academic and career opportunities. This lesson provides a student-centered opportunity for students to explore future pathways while also supporting a smooth and consistent implementation to our new ACL testing process. It gives us the opportunity to create a shared future-ready experience across all middle schools. Every student will have the chance to learn about the programs and opportunities

available in LCPS. Again, they'll be able to engage with SchooLinks and reflect on their interests and strengths through the Riasec framework. Ultimately, this work supports our broader goal of helping students make informed decisions as they prepare for high school, college, career, and life. Now I will turn it over to my colleague, Dr. Grubbs, to discuss the Riasec model. Thank you, Ms. Clark. I'm going to talk about the Riasec model, and although we are

going to introduce this as a new model in LCPS, the Riasec framework has been around since the '60s. The Riasec framework is embedded in things like ASVAB, it's embedded into Sology. And while we've used it for over 50 years, what we have not done is the discussed component of Riasec. We've used the assessed components. And so on our next slide, I'm going to take you all through an activity. We're going to do one letter. We're not going to do the entire framework. But the-- Well, we can always find more time.

Really, Riasec is creating pathways for students. The model we've been using in career development has been showcasing how much you could earn in a specific career and trying to work backwards from there. Where this model is very much about meeting students where they are. It's not about what do I want to be, it really is more about who I am, where do I fit in, how can I add value? So Riasec on the next slide, it's actually not an acronym. The R stands for realistic, I stands for investigative, A

stands for artistic, S stands for social, E stands for enterprising, and C stands for conventional. What I want to note here is that those six letters actually are already mapped back to all the careers that are out there through the Department of Labor. And so from a career pathway perspective, we can actually map our courses, our program pathways, all back to these six letters. So on the next slide, we're going to only unpack one letter, which is R for

realistic. I'm going to ask that you take a pen or pencil out, and as I go through this slide, I'm going to ask that you take tally marks for anything that resonates with you that aligns to your skills, your values, or your interests. Realistic folks are doers. So if you're a doer, you can make a tally mark. They like to work with machines, tools, plants, animals, or the environment.

They may like to build and repair things. They may be physically active. They may be into the outdoors. They may work with animals. And they may like to operate tools and machines. I say may because I may not like to work with animals, but I may be physically active. I may like to build and repair things. And just because I don't like to work with one aspect doesn't mean that I'm not more realistic than my colleague next to me.

I also encourage you to look at the visual and look at the icons, and for every visual, make another tally mark for something that resonates with you. So there's someone planting something, there's a picture of tools, there's a crane, and there's someone that is running hurdles. So if any of you, if you see anything in you, make a tally mark. On the next slide, if we could advance, this is a video. I don't think we're going to play the-- All right, we can play the

video. Thank you. As we watch the video, every letter is about a one-minute video, and so we would take students through all six letters. As you watch the video, I'm going to ask that you make tally marks for what you hear, what you see, and what resonates with you. So we will play the video. Identify with a realistic theme, see themselves as practical, mechanical, and active. They enjoy hands-on activities, which may include working with animals,

tools, or machines. In their spare time, they may enjoy activities including mechanics, gardening, hunting or fishing, carpentry, making jewelry, playing sports, driving vehicles, skydiving, or landscaping. You can often find people that align with a realistic theme in outdoor settings, in national parks, athletic facilities, farms or greenhouses, or in the military.

Some of the greatest skills they possess include building and repairing, using tools and equipment, concrete problem-solving, growing plants, and anything involving manual dexterity, public safety, and engineering and technology. They tend to value things you can see, touch, and use in their life, and often want their work to be hands-on, physical, and fairly active. Thank you. We'll go to the next slide.

Let me show you how to make a cold pack and a hot- In addition to the videos, students will have visual representation of each letter. What you will notice about the video and the illustrations is that there's no discussion of careers. We have flipped the conversation around career development to who you are as a person versus how much a specific career can make, biases that you have about a field or profession, and it's really centering the student in this work in terms of career development.

The other thing that I want to share, which is so powerful with Katie's lesson and the work that she's doing, is that it does not put career counseling just in the office of CTE or just in the office of school counseling. This work is really putting career conversations into every single classroom at the middle school level, and we're going to impact 16,000 kids around how are you connecting with what you're learning in the classroom to your future career and who you are. Research has shown that we tend to gravitate towards two to three letters, and so

while we didn't go through all five letters today, I am curious how your tally marks turned out and if you are realistic or if we need to come back and do five more letters. I only had four in this one. I had 18. Oh, okay. All right. There you go. All right, so- I really like Legos and gardening, so and IKEA furniture, which is grown up Legos. There's five more letters, so make sure y'all can come back and find which letter you lead with. Yeah, you should've done social. Then we would've been 5,000.

C is conventional. Investigative. Oh, yeah. Thank you. Well, we had the benefit of doing it as the full board- Yes ... before you got here. Yeah. And so that was really, really fun. Go ahead, continue All right. Thanks, Dr. Grubbs. And as he mentioned, this is really exciting that we're tying it all together for our students here in LCPS. And to go off of that, it is a really exciting time in LCPS with all the diverse programs and opportunities we offer our students, and we're hoping this lesson will

help with that awareness. The lesson will begin by introducing students to all of our special programs. So they are going to hear voices of our current students who are participating in them as of today through videos, and students will learn about each program, and they will engage in reflection activities designed to help them think about their own interests, strengths, and future aspirations. Our goal is to ensure that every student is aware of all the opportunities

available to them and can begin seeing how these opportunities connect to their own future plans. So to ensure students and families can continue to access these resources beyond November 12th, the lesson is being developed as a Schoology course. This will provide ongoing access to the videos, reflection activities, and information about the various special programs and pathways available in LCPS. There will also be a folder in there for families, so after the lesson, they can go

home and talk about this with their families. Students will also have dedicated time at the end of the lesson to further explore the programs and opportunities that interest them most. Our goal ultimately is for students to leave the experience with a greater awareness of the programs available to them and a better understanding of how those opportunities connect to them personally. We have also been working closely with school counseling, who've been an excellent

partner, and we are planning to link each program's School Links page within the Schoology course. This gives students an easy way to continue exploring any program that interests them and learn more about the opportunities available. Our hope is that students will leave this lesson curious and empowered to dig deeper into pathways that connect with their interests and future aspirations outside of the school day. So that concludes our presentation.

We'd love to hear any questions, feedback, considerations you think we should keep in mind as we continue implementing this district-wide experience. Awesome. Thank you guys so much. Mr. Pepper? This is fantastic. A couple questions, then I'm going to dive into your overarching feedback question here. Going back to the testing at the very beginning, how was the date chosen? Just

out of curiosity, why was it November 12th, you said? So typically, we test over three Saturdays throughout end of October into November. We did work with the middle school office to pick a date that wasn't impacting other activities within the school, so we did work collaboratively with the middle school office to select that date. Just putting it out there, there's also a day the high school's testing all day for

SAT and PSAT. It might be a good day to combine those two, just get all our testing done in one fell swoop. Just putting it out there. This is the same test for all the academies, is that correct? Dr. Clark, is it the same test for all the academies? Yes. It's one test for AET and AOS, so students that apply to both, it's the same test.

Do students identify on the test which one they're thinking of, or is it just luck of the draw? Great question. So students have to apply before October 16th, and they have to apply for one or both. So when they apply, they're indicating for AOS, and then they also would have to apply for AET as well. And then when they take the test, they're taking that assessment, and then that is used for the admissions cycle.

Okay. No, appreciate you're doing it this way. It's much more equitable for our students to do it this way. Let's talk about the RISAC for a little bit. That's super cool. Sorry, I missed the whole find your RISAC. It looks like I might be a realist. Really like that we're moving away from the idea of "Let's pick a career based on how much I make," and then I decide I want to go into that career, and I'm completely miserable, like many doctors I know. Or lawyers.

But I really like this model. When we talk about it's embedded into Schoology, I assume that's the Schoology course that you guys were talking about when you said that the RISAC's embedded into Schoology. I can lean in first. Yeah. So as an assessment, it's built into School Links through, I think, a "Would You Rather" assessment that's in School Links. On the front end, students don't even realize they're doing RISAC. It's more on the assessment on the back end, how they're mapping the careers and things like that. Now through the lesson, that's where we're having the conversation about the six

different letters, and that's the piece that's been missed over the last 50 to 60 years. It's do a survey, but there's been no connection to the letters. The letters are really mapped back on the back end of the careers that students are exposed to. Does that make sense? Yes. It's very helpful. And then so when they do the Schoology course, because you said it's a Schoology course, is it asynchronous, hybrid? I know there's probably an at-home component that students are going to likely have to do.

Great question. If we can slide back a couple slides. One more, I think. So right here- Yeah ... this is an example. So each of our programs will have its own page. As you can see there, this is mapped to the I, the S, and the R, and there's going to be information for each program. So these will be here. Students will have time to explore these. They're going to be asked "What was one of your top letters? Explore that." And then they're going to have some discussion time in class, and

then they're going to go back. Maybe what's a program in a letter that maybe you didn't score as high? Because we definitely want to make sure kids know that RISAC is just a tool, and it doesn't mean you can't explore other programs that aren't necessarily in one of your top letters. And then there will be family resources in there, so families could continue to have discussions about this. I do believe counseling is also working on expanding this into their lessons after November 12th.

And then to answer your other question, it's going to happen synchronously through our teachers in the classroom. So they'll take students through one letter at a time, very similar to how I did it with you, a little bit more in-depth, a little bit longer, but they're going to take kids through one at a time. And then students can come back asynchronously and explore after the class. I like that. I'd love to see what the Schoology course looks like when it's all up and running, as someone who spends his day building Schoology courses all day long. And then, so kind of to answer your overarching question, then I'm going to let my

chair maybe get her piece in. But what's a consideration we should keep in mind? A couple big things. One of them is teacher training and buy-in, right? So as teachers are presenting this, what you don't want is you don't want our middle school students to have vastly different experiences simply based on who's delivering this content. So we want to make sure that what are the considerations that we have for our teachers to be trained to implement this day, to do this with fidelity, to ensure

that our students come out of it with the right model. And then the other thing is, if this is successful, what is that going to mean for enrollment, and lottery, and pool, and all those other things? Because if we do this right, I would envision that would pique a lot of interest in many more students than we currently have applying now. So I'll answer a few of that. So we have thought about teacher training.

We did a sample lesson with all the principals and their contact leads. Each school identified a lead for this lesson. We already did that. We got some initial feedback. We walked them through like a student. What do we need to change? What do we need to do differently? And luckily, we have our November 2nd and 3rd days coming up, our work days. So our principals are planning on taking some of that portion of the day to walk staff through this and make sure they have all the resources they need.

We really are trying to design it so that anybody could pick this up and lead the lesson. It should be that easy to deliver. So that is our hope. They'll have a facilitator guide, and they should be able to walk through pretty easily the lesson. That's great. Thank you so much. I am very excited about this. I have been excited about this shift for a long time. I was actually with a group of youth this weekend who are seniors, and they're

getting ready to go off to college. I was just listening in on their conversation about whether they should find something they're passionate about that may not make a lot of money or whether they should just try to go big for go in finance and find something really that will pay the bills. And it was a fascinating conversation, and like I said, I was just kind of listening, and it really reminded me why this is so important, because

so many of the kids were coming back to what they were good at and what fulfills them and what their passions are, and this is really what we want to see as a career path. We want something that they can sustain, that they're going to love to do. So I love this shift. I think it's exciting. I think kids will glob onto it, and it will be interesting to see the data from last year's interest to this year's interest and if we can tie any of that to this

experience. My first question is for the Schoology course and letting parents know, is that going to go home in a community message where it's like, "Today was November 12th. All your students had this lesson. Here's the information." Is that something we're envisioning? Great questions. We've been working with communications. They're going to do a web story on this to get it out, and then we're also going to provide that to each individual school, so they can include that in their newsletters- Okay

... prior to November 12th. We do have a flyer that we've asked principals to start including into their newsletters as well about ACL testing and the Future Ready lesson. So we do have plans for communicating that out and then also follow up after. Awesome. Make sure they know to continue the conversation at home. For sure. And then I'm guessing all letters are represented in our programs. Yes? Yes. All of them are mapped to the three different letters.

So all of our letters represent programs. Yeah. And then my other question is just sort of a devil's advocate question. As our students sit in these lessons, and this is going to be appealing to them, this is about who they are, so that's going to resonate, I think, on some level. But not every kid needs to go to a program, and that's not the right fit for every kid, and there aren't enough slots for kids to do that here in LCPS.

So how are we framing the conversation outside of just tying it to our programs? Okay. I'll start, and then Dr. Grubbs can add in. We are going to have an intro video. We're going to make sure that's emphasized that there might not be a program that you're interested in, and that's okay. But our purpose here is to make sure they're at least aware of the opportunities. And then Dr. Grubbs, myself, and Heather Ross from school counseling, we plan on

closing it out with a video to the students, just to really make sure students know that if you don't choose a program and you go to your regular high school, there's a lot of great opportunities there as well. We do see that this lesson might expand in the future as we continue to build. Obviously, this is phase one. It's our first year implementing this, but really even customizing it per cluster with what they have offered at their home high school. So I think there's a lot of opportunity for us to continue to improve this

as we move forward. And I think to Katie's point, we're mapping all of our CT courses to this as well. So all of our courses are mapped to the six letters. We're fine-tuning some of that. I think this opens the door, too. We can map our clubs to these letters, whether you're signing up for dual enrollment or IB. This will be on just pathway discussions. This is, "Why am I taking this? Why am I applying to this college?" I think it's part of a larger conversation around skills, values, and interests.

Yeah, even just in the elective world, there are so many opportunities. Obviously, something we've talked about and we're going to talk about is the arts, and I would hate for a kid to have to sit there and be like, "There's nothing for me." So making sure that we're getting that message out and maybe even touching on, maybe it's not a program, but maybe it's an elective. Because certainly all of these letters are represented in the many, many, many elective choices, too many, that we have in LCPS.

It's competitive for that. So I think kids understanding that, too, is really great. And extracurriculars. These kids can literally do it all. Really, we have every opportunity here. I worry that it'll get funneled into, "Well, I can't use my skills if I'm not in a program, or if I'm not in CTE, or if I'm not..." But every kid has to take an elective. Every kid has access to athletics and after-school curricular activities.

So I think that tying that message in would be something that I would ask and recommend, and I do have it on my calendar, so I'm really hoping to get into a classroom to see it in action. So, I will look forward to seeing how this evolves. This is awesome. Anything else, Mr. Pepper? Okay. All right. IB Programming. And so that will be Ms. Katie Clark as well, so I will pass it over again. Oh, and Mr. Jeff Roundsley is also joining us. And Mr. Schaefer is joining us. And Mr. Schaefer is joining us. I'll kick us off, though. So, back in September, we brought some elementary options, and we were asked to bring back some more information about the PYP, MYP, and the elementary arts integrated learning.

So we are back today, and our agenda, we're going to first talk about the arts integrated learning, and then we're going to move into the PYP and MYP. So I'm going to turn it right over to Mr. Roundsley to talk about the elementary arts integrated learning. All right. Thank you, Ms. Clark. So we are first going to talk about a proposal for what an arts integrated program in our elementary schools might look like. This is based on visits to schools in Fairfax County, talking with the

administration at Bailey's Elementary School for the Arts and Sciences, and also a lot of research for schools around the country for how they approach this. And this represents just some initial thinking around what a program like this might look like. So on the next slide, and slide after that, we have three big grounding ideas that are important that we have found in arts integrated programs. The first one is that it's not just more art or more music,

but that that art and music is grounded in content, and that it is a way that students learn. So it's embedded within core instruction, and there's really strong collaboration and opportunities for collaboration between our art and music and potentially theater teachers, and also our classroom teachers. The second one is that these programs give students lots of opportunities to show what they know in different ways. So voice and choice and lots of ways that they

express their learning through performance and creation and movement, and artistic expression, not just the standard ways that we measure and look at learning. And the third one is that this represents pathways for students and really contributes to a sense of belonging in our schools, that students feel connected to what's happening, and that it's also a way that students can see pathways in the arts that might serve into our secondary programs, and continue students on a pathway towards looking at the arts as a way that they can discover their

interests, think critically, solve problems, and collaborate and find some joy and some connection in that. So those are our three big philosophies, and three things that we would really want to see in a program here in Loudoun is first, that we, again, connect the arts and academics, that we intentionally plan lots of ways for our art and music and theater arts teachers to work with classroom teachers and truly integrate the learning that happens

there. That was definitely something that our teams in Fairfax that we spoke to talked to us about. Oh, sorry, we're on the next slide, Morgan. And then next is that there's lots of outreach to our community and partnerships. So we saw at Hunter's Woods representations of the work that artists and residents did, and working with students to express their learning in different ways, and that students have lots of opportunities to not just work with

practicing artists in our classrooms, but also to have connections to really relevant and authentic experiences and field trips. And the third one is that there's a culminating experience, either some sort of artistic creation or a performance or some way that students exhibit their learning and showcase their learning. So those are the big ideas that we were grappling with as we thought about what this might look like, and now we have a few ideas around what a proposal for this might look like.

These are just initial thinking and really some big priorities that we know are important. So first, we know that we would need someone to help lead this work, so we have a proposal to create an elementary arts program coordinator who could help guide this in some schools that are piloting this for us.
